newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds, dollar rebound from Friday's losses.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds, dollar rebound from Friday's losses.

text.p: Stocks, bonds and the dollar rose Monday as the markets recovered from Friday's panic at Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments and saw no threat of a interest rate hike by the U.S. central bank.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 82.00 points at 6,463.94, its biggest point gain since a 97-point rise on Nov. 6 in a post-election euphoria.
The Nasdaq Composite index set a record, gaining 28.59 points 1,316.27, surpassing the old record of 1,300.37 set on Dec. 3.

On Friday, the Dow lost 55 points after Greenspan's warning about "irrational exuberance" in financial markets was viewed as a hint that the central bank might resort to higher interest rates to slow the ascent of financial markets.
At one time Friday, the world's most closely watched stock index tumbled nearly 145 points -- its steepest drop since July 15 when it tumbled 161.05 points.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines 1,919 to 632 on heavy volume of 381 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
"The underlying fundamental is that Greenspan is not in a position to raise rates," said Marshall Acuff, portfolio strategist at Smith Barney.

Investors sensed that they had overreacted to the Fed chief's comments, which were made in a speech delivered Thursday night, and there was a consensus that Greenspan would have a tough time justifying an interest rate increase as the economy slowed.

"I think Greenspan is saying he wants us to be cautious, not comfortable about where the market is right now. Cautious does not mean bearish," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker.
"What we're seeing in the Dow and S&P 500 is a continuation of the snapback we saw Friday," he said.
The bond market also bounced back, with the benchmark 30-year Treasury up 20/32, or $6.25 on a $1,000 bond, sending its yield down to 6.47 percent from 6.54 percent at Friday's close.
In late New York trading, the dollar settled at 1.5577 German marks and 113.50 Japanese yen, well above 1.5465 marks and 112.88 yen late Friday.
Oil prices fell after the United Nations cleared Iraq to begin limited sales of crude for the first time since the start of the Gulf War.
Warm weather forecasts for the central United States also eased concerns about tight natural gas and heating oil supplies heading into the strong winter demand season.
Crude oil for January delivery fell 32 cents to $25.30 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange, up from the day's low of $25.

January heating oil sank 2.53 cents to 72.13 cents a gallon, and January natural gas lost 26.5 cents to $3.222 per 1,000 cubic feet. January unleaded gasoline dropped 0.92 cent to 68.88 cents a gallon.

Soybean prices fell sharply on the Chicago Board of Trade on a slowdown in U.S. bean exports and beneficial rains in South America's soybean fields. January soybeans lost 7.25 cents at $6.88-3/4 a bushel.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index jumped 48.6 points to 4,011.6. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 surged 327.01 points to 20,603.71.
